summary: This experimental specification proposes a protocol for creating symmetric encryption keys shared by a whole group and for handing them out to the peers who need them. It is the protocol companion to the architecture described in RFC 2094.

plainLanguage.summary: GKMP specifies how a controller creates symmetric keys for a group and distributes them to members. Its messages let participants check permissions and replace keys when the group changes.

subtitle: An experimental protocol for creating shared group keys and distributing them to authorized members.

tldr.problem: Pairwise key management lets two parties share a key, but a communicating group needs more than two members to use common symmetric keys.
tldr.mechanism: A group controller and a first member cooperate to create group keys. The controller then establishes a one-time key with each other member and uses it to deliver the group keys after checking signed permissions.
tldr.outcome: The specification covers group creation, rekeying, member joins and deletion. RFC 2093 is Experimental and does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: The Need for Group Keys
sections.content:
The RFC describes physical key distribution as costly and slow. Cooperative key-management methods can create pairwise keys, but the memo addresses groups that need shared keys for communication among more than two hosts.

The Group Key Management Protocol (GKMP) is an application-layer protocol. It creates symmetric keys for a group and distributes them to qualified members, and can use multicast when available.
sections.plainLanguage: GKMP manages keys shared by a group instead of only keys shared between two hosts. It defines messages for creating, distributing and changing those keys.

sections.title: Controllers, Members and Permissions
sections.content:
A group controller creates and distributes keys, starts key changes and collects acknowledgments. Other group members help create keys, check the controller's authority, accept keys and keep local compromise information.

A signed group token identifies the group, controller, action, permissions, rekey interval and token version. Permission certificates are signed by a higher authority. Members compare the stated permissions with the requested service and deny the service if permission is insufficient.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller manages the group's keys, while members verify its authority and check the permissions in signed credentials. A compromise list helps members identify hosts that should no longer participate.

sections.title: Creating and Distributing Group Keys
sections.content:
For group creation, the controller and first member exchange four messages to create the group traffic encryption key (GTEK) and group key encryption key (GKEK). Each contributes information to the key creation process, and the messages carry signatures that let the other party check identity and authorization.

For every other member, the controller and member create a session key encryption key (SKEK). The controller sends the group keys encrypted with that SKEK, and the member checks the group information and acknowledges successful decryption. This distribution process uses six messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller and first member exchange information to create the group's keys. The controller then establishes a separate temporary key with each other member and encrypts the group keys for delivery.

sections.title: Rekeying, Joining and Removing Members
sections.content:
To rekey a group, the controller and first member create new group keys. The controller then multicasts one signed rekey message encrypted with the current GKEK, allowing members that hold the current key to validate the change.

A member-initiated join adds a request before the normal individual key-distribution exchange. Cooperative deletion asks a member to remove its keys and acknowledge. If a member is hostile or compromised, the specification describes creating a new group without it and switching group operations to the new keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Members can receive new group keys, request to join, or be asked to delete their keys. If a member cannot be trusted, the controller can create a replacement group without that member.

sections.title: Compromise and Operational Choices
sections.content:
The RFC says the document in its entirety concerns security. It describes a trade-off when a member is found to be compromised: stopping all group traffic may protect the group, while continuing traffic may preserve an important operation.

GKMP checks a revocation list during group creation and supports creating a replacement group without compromised members. The RFC does not prescribe whether a group must stop operating when a compromised member is present.
sections.plainLanguage: A compromised member may know the group's keys. The protocol helps exclude that member from a new group, but the decision to stop current communications is left to the group.
